					<description><![CDATA[<p>As AI clusters push beyond rack-scale limits, optical interconnects and circuit switching are reshaping how data centers scale. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/coppers-grip-on-ai-scaling-is-starting-to-slip/">Copper’s Grip On AI Scaling Is Starting To Slip</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span><b><span data-contrast="none">Key Takeaways:</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<ul>
<li><span data-contrast="none">Scale-up may go beyond one rack and may use optical interconnects for longer runs.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></li>
<li><span data-contrast="none">Optical circuit switching may expand beyond Google.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></li>
<li><span data-contrast="none">Scale-in is a new scaling term referring to the scale of a single server board.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p><span data-contrast="none">Data-center network fabrics are undergoing another architectural shift as optical interconnects assume a larger role in AI-cluster connectivity, extending into scale-up domains and influencing overall topology design.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">Scale-up has typically been defined as a single rack with copper interconnect, with programmers using memory semantics. That definition is getting fuzzier.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">“The old rule that scale-up is copper and scale-out is optical is starting to blur,” said Steven Woo, fellow and distinguished inventor at </span><a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/rambus-inc/">Rambus</a><span data-contrast="none">. “As data rates climb inside the rack, copper is running into physical limits around loss, reach, and power, challenging the ability of copper within a rack. From a signaling standpoint, optics can offer a cleaner scaling path at high data rates but must do so with manageable power and reliability over relatively short distances.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">Lower latency drives all of this because GPUs underuse their capacity when they wait for data. “There have been a lot of reports on the efficiency of these GPUs that are maybe 25% efficient because they&#8217;re just sitting there waiting for data,” said Eric Aguilar, CEO and cofounder of Omnitron.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">Google, meanwhile, implemented an optical circuit switching (OCS) network with a torus configuration, and others are also considering OCS networks for other network architectures.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">This architectural shift also requires a more precise assessment of how scaling terminology is evolving across AI data-center networks.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p aria-level="1"><b><span data-contrast="none">Scaling evolves yet further<br />
</span></b><span data-contrast="none">With an ever-shifting hierarchy of data-center scaling, particularly for AI workloads, this has rolled out as scale-up, scale-out, and scale-across approaches.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">More recently, scale-in has shown up. “This is a new term that has only started in the last three months,” said Vishal Chandrasekar, head of product management at </span><a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/ayar-labs/">Ayar Labs</a><span data-contrast="none">. “It refers to the amount of bandwidth coming out of the GPU that stays within a single chassis.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">The definitions of these, up until recently, can be summed up as follows:</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<ul>
<li>Scale-in is between processors in a single server or on a single board.<span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></li>
<li><span data-contrast="none">Scale-up is within a rack, wired using copper, and allows programming using memory semantics. (Spoiler alert: this is now out of date.)</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></li>
<li><span data-contrast="none">Scale-out is between racks and employs Ethernet RDMA semantics. It increasingly uses optical interconnect.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></li>
<li><span data-contrast="none">Scale-across is between different data-center campuses and involves fiber.</span></li>
</ul>
<p><span data-contrast="none">Aside from the addition of scale-in, scale-up is evolving. Computing clusters are growing beyond the bounds of a single rack, recruiting servers in adjacent racks. Now the interconnect distance is longer, and copper may no longer be the best medium. As a result, fiber is percolating into scale-up.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">“If it&#8217;s going to be within a rack, you&#8217;re probably going to use copper,” explained Chandrasekar. “If it&#8217;s adjacent racks, you&#8217;re on the margin, but let&#8217;s say you stick with copper. If you&#8217;re going into anything more than adjacent racks, you&#8217;re going to go with optics.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">In terms of how long a link requires optics, “Assuming they&#8217;re using a 200-gig signaling rate, copper probably makes sense up to five or, if you really push it, seven meters,” Chandrasekar explained. “Certainly, once you hit 10 meters and beyond, it absolutely has to be optics.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">Scale-up, as previously defined, had three elements: single rack, copper, and memory semantics. The first two are now being phased out, and the remaining defining factor is the use of memory semantics.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">“Software guys define scale-up as one operating system domain where they have one memory,” said Priyank Shukla, director of product management, interface IP at </span><a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a><span data-contrast="none">. “So, if you&#8217;re running a process, the processor can write to one memory location, regardless of where that memory is.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">Typical implementations of scale-up and scale-out minimize the number of hops. “Within the scale-up domain, every GPU is just one hop away from every other GPU,” said Chandrasekar. “If you&#8217;re talking scale-out, it&#8217;s like two hops.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240,&quot;469777462&quot;:[8595],&quot;469777927&quot;:[0],&quot;469777928&quot;:[1]}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">The one-hop expectation for scale-up is enforced by the new UALink standard. “UALink scale-up fabrics are designed to maintain single-switch-hop accelerator-to-accelerator connectivity,” explained Shukla. “Even as a scale-up domain expands beyond a single rack, communication between accelerators is intended to traverse only a single UALink switch. As a result, connecting accelerators across racks does not inherently require a switch-to-switch topology that would introduce an additional hop. The single switch can be located in different places within the rack architecture, such as a Top of Rack (ToR) or Middle of Rack (MoR) deployment, but the key point is that accelerator traffic still traverses only one switch between endpoints.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240,&quot;469777462&quot;:[8595],&quot;469777927&quot;:[0],&quot;469777928&quot;:[1]}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="auto">Once scale-up domains extend beyond the rack, the same latency and hop-count constraints shift attention from interconnect media to the broader network topology that links accelerators, switches, and servers.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="none">Network architectures</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;134245418&quot;:true,&quot;134245529&quot;:true,&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559738&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"><br />
</span><span data-contrast="none">The way servers are interconnected in the data center makes a power and performance difference, but there’s no single correct configuration. Different workloads benefit from different arrangements.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">One of the most common is called a Clos or leaf-and-spine network. Given two servers, there’s a short path between them. While this architecture is pervasive, one of the biggest players is using something else for its AI network.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">“Google doesn&#8217;t have a leaf and spine network,” observed Chandrasekar. “It&#8217;s a torus network, which means every TPU is linked to adjacent TPUs, adjacent in three directions: up, down, and to the right, giving it a systolic character.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-large wp-image-24279990" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-7.gif?resize=830%2C1024&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="830" height="1024" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-7.gif?resize=830%2C1024&amp;ssl=1 830w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-7.gif?resize=243%2C300&amp;ssl=1 243w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-7.gif?resize=768%2C948&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-7.gif?resize=600%2C741&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 830px) 100vw, 830px" /></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="none">Fig. </span></b><b><span data-contrast="none">1:</span></b><b><span data-contrast="none"> Network architectures. The top shows leaf-and-spine, with a one-hop path from any server to any server. Below is a torus, which requires more hops between any two servers. Source: Bryon Moyer/Semiconductor Engineering</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">A key difference between the two is the number of hops necessary to get from any server to any other. With leaf-and-spine, it’s one. With a torus, it depends on the locations. The path above shows four hops.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">“If you want to get from one GPU on one end to another GPU on the other end, you have lots of hops along the way,” Chandrasekar noted. A long-enough path can be implemented with optical for better power/performance. But each hop brings some inefficiency since the typical way these networks are built involves packet switching. Packets contain artifacts in their headers that must be inspected at each switch or router.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">Optical technology doesn’t understand packets. So, the four-hop path above would require, at each hop, that the optical signal be converted to electrical. Once in the electrical domain, the next hop can be determined, but before the signal makes that next hop, it has to be converted back to optical.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">These repeated conversions at each node hurt latency and consume a fair bit of energy. Is there a better way to build optical networks?</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p aria-level="1"><b><span data-contrast="none">Circuit switching is old school</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;134245418&quot;:true,&quot;134245529&quot;:true,&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559738&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"><br />
</span><span data-contrast="none">Packet switching is taken for granted today, but it’s not the original network. Previously, there were nationwide telephone systems that used circuit switches. Circuit switching means opening up an entire path from source to destination and giving exclusive use to one flow. In the old days, this flow was the conversation between the people at both ends of the line. Party lines aside, no one else could use that line while the conversation was busy.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">An analogy helps here. Let’s say you want to take a road trip from Los Angeles to Boston. In real life, you’d share the road with many other vehicles, and at each intersection or interchange, you and everyone else have an opportunity to change your route to get to your specific destination. Now, as anyone who has ever been held up by a traffic light knows, such travel would be so much easier if everyone else would go away and leave the road to you.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">If you were to reserve the entire path from LA to Boston, eliminating all stops, you could get there much more quickly and efficiently. This is what a circuit-switched network provides. It comes with a slower background network that configures the path before enabling the conversation. For the phone system, the most recent of these is called Signaling System 7.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">The problem is that even while you’re still in California, no one else can be on any of the other roads along the way, even right outside Boston. Only when you’d arrived would those roads be freed up for someone else’s trip, which sounds inefficient.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p aria-level="1"><b><span data-contrast="none">Packets to the rescue… for some things</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;134245418&quot;:true,&quot;134245529&quot;:true,&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559738&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"><br />
</span><span data-contrast="none">This is where packet switching came in, which can be thought of as the stop signs, stop lights, and highway interchanges that allow multiple people to make multiple trips to completely different destinations, all while using roads that others are also using. Replace those intersections with routers and the roads with wires, and you have the essence of a packet-switched network, which has become the standard for most of networking.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">What’s new is the data center challenge of repeated conversions between optical and electrical domains, due to packet routing. “Data moves by picking a fat, infinite-bandwidth fiber signal, putting it into an electrical switch, converting that optical signal to an electrical signal, reading the packet, and then routing it to another GPU,” explained Aguilar. “That optical-electrical-optical loop burns an enormous amount of power, adds latency, and drives up cost in data centers. About 15 years ago, Google started looking at this, and about 10 years ago, made it happen with a MEMS [microelectromechanical systems]-based optical circuit switch.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">The company uses nothing but adjustable MEMS mirrors at each router. Those mirrors reflect the laser light coming from the source fiber onto the destination fiber for that particular route. Those are set up at every node to provide a clear path from source to destination, with no conversions necessary. This approach is called optical circuit switching (OCS).</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p aria-level="1"><b><span data-contrast="none">Google’s implementation</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;134245418&quot;:true,&quot;134245529&quot;:true,&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559738&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"><br />
</span><span data-contrast="none">Google has found OCS beneficial. “We have spent the last eight years deeply integrating OCS and wave division multiplexing (WDM) into Jupiter [their network],” noted author Amin Vahdat, senior vice president and chief technologist, AI and Infrastructure at </span>Google<span data-contrast="none">, in a paper from 2022. “The combination of OCS with our software-defined networking (SDN) architecture has enabled new capabilities: support for incremental network builds with heterogeneous technologies; higher performance and lower latency, cost, and power consumption; real-time application priority and communication patterns; and zero-downtime upgrades. Jupiter does all this while reducing flow completion by 10%, improving throughput by 30%, using 40% less power, incurring 30% less cost, and delivering 50× less downtime than the best-known alternatives.”</span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">The power savings reflect a number of changes. “You&#8217;re eliminating half of the transceivers, eliminating the liquid cooling that&#8217;s required, and then the ASIC/electronics that are in the switch itself, and you&#8217;re replacing that with an optical solution,” said Aguilar.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">In an OCS, when a large chunk of data must flow between two servers, first the background network configures the mirrors all along the route, then the flow can proceed with no conversions or routing decisions. The key here, however, is that this data all comes from the same place and goes to the same place. None of the data can branch off and travel to a different node. That makes this an optimization that’s workload-specific.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">If this approach were taken for short, frequent bursts of data, more time would be spent setting up the routes and tearing them down than sending data. Using the road analogy, reserving the whole road from LA to Boston might make sense if there is a convoy that is longer than the full route. In that case, no one else can use the road while it’s occupied, but no part of it is sitting idle. This is similar to long data flows that warrant OCS.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">“Optical circuit switching makes sense for ‘elephant flows,’ a term that I&#8217;ve been hearing others use,” said Aguilar. “It&#8217;s much better than these bursts of ‘mouse flows.’ This is more for AI and large language-model learning and inferencing.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="auto">And since OCS depends on reserving an end-to-end optical path before payload transmission begins, its effectiveness also depends on the control plane that configures those paths.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;335559739&quot;:0}"> </span></p>
<p aria-level="1"><b><span data-contrast="none">A new Signaling System</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;134245418&quot;:true,&quot;134245529&quot;:true,&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559738&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"><br />
</span><span data-contrast="none">A background network configures the mirrors when the flow is set up. Analogous to Signaling System 7, it’s a slow Ethernet-based control network running alongside the optical network. “You have a lower-bandwidth Ethernet network to reconfigure the switches and the data route,” said Aguilar.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">It doesn’t take too long to reconfigure the network, but it does take time, which is another reason this makes sense only for long flows. Even so, configuring the network isn’t what limits how long a new configuration can be up and running. “It&#8217;s the transceiver lock that&#8217;s the bottleneck,” said Aguilar.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">It may seem more complex to replace one network with two, but the control network isn’t complex. “You still have Ethernet that connects rack to rack to route the pipes to the right spots, but it&#8217;s a simpler, more elegant solution,” he said. It also doesn’t add significantly to capital costs. “Ethernet switches are cheap. The Ethernet switch is just a simple low-bandwidth command center.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p aria-level="1"><b><span data-contrast="none">Mixing packet and circuit</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;134245418&quot;:true,&quot;134245529&quot;:true,&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559738&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"><br />
</span><span data-contrast="none">The torus network in Figure 1 above uses point-to-point connections, and circuit switching benefits the many-hop connections. But the leaf/spine architecture is different: it features switches and routers. Could this architecture benefit from OCS as well?</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">In the torus example, the flows are end-to-end. This could be done in a leaf/spine setup as well, although fewer hops mean less power savings. What some companies are reviewing is whether, for instance, the top tier of a leaf/spine network could be an OCS, with the source and destination routers accepting multiple packets on the input side, bundling them together for optical transport to the destination router, where the packets are extracted and finally sent, electrically, to their final nodes.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">“OCS optical will terminate into a switch, and then after that, it&#8217;s electrical,” said Synopsys’ Shukla.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-large wp-image-24279991" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-6.gif?resize=765%2C1024&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="765" height="1024" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-6.gif?resize=765%2C1024&amp;ssl=1 765w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-6.gif?resize=224%2C300&amp;ssl=1 224w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-6.gif?resize=768%2C1028&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-6.gif?resize=600%2C803&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 765px) 100vw, 765px" /></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="none">Fig. </span></b><b><span data-contrast="none">2</span></b><b><span data-contrast="none">: Mixing circuit and packet switching. The top portion illustrates an end-to-end circuit in a tree-style network. If the optical path were limited to the router-to-router connection, then packets could be assembled in the source router and disassembled and rerouted electrically in the destination router. </span></b><b><span data-contrast="none">Source: Bryon Moyer/Semiconductor Engineering</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">As long as the traffic is steady enough, with multiple packets from the source side targeting nodes connected to the final router, then it could make sense to open an optical path between the two switches. As shown in Figure 2, this may look somewhat trivial, but if the path between routers is complex and goes through many nodes, such a circuit could make sense.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">Google’s OCS is a done deal, and in fact, they’re moving from a torus network to yet another configuration called a dragonfly. Other companies have yet to deploy such a network, whether torus or some other tree-style option, but word on the street is that OCS is being considered by different companies for different networks.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">“People are looking at that saying, ‘Can we use that technology in leaf and spine structures to replace the second layer with an OCS while keeping the first layer cloud packet switching?’” said Chandrasekar.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">The initial switchover to optical is manageable. “There isn&#8217;t a significant overhaul in a data center to make this happen,” said Aguilar. “If I can retrofit my data centers with this solution, I can reduce the power demand, or I can increase capacity in existing data centers.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">Once an optical network is in place, it doesn’t need further upgrades. The fiber has no idea what generation of transceiver, memory, or processor is in use, so changing those generations doesn’t require changing the network.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">This idea is still being mulled over in the industry. “It&#8217;s more in the exploratory phase right now,” Chandrasekar added. “No one&#8217;s deployed it.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p aria-level="1"><b><span data-contrast="none">Optical encroaches further</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;134245418&quot;:true,&quot;134245529&quot;:true,&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559738&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"><br />
</span><span data-contrast="none">Both developments involve increasing optical participation in the data center. With scale-up, it’s now joining copper for the longest connections, making the complete set of scale-up connections a mix of copper and fiber.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">Optical standards will help. “The OCP is trying to define the standards so that everyone can play in the ecosystem,” said Aguilar. “Google has developed a lot of proprietary aspects, and it needs to be standardized for this to be adopted, or it won&#8217;t work right.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span><span data-contrast="none">If this takes off, will it stress optical suppliers with a sudden burst of demand? Aguilar doesn’t think so, based on planned production scaling and industry mergers. “For the next five years, based on our projections, we&#8217;re okay,” he said. “Our foundry partner is already scaling as a result of the expectation of growth, while Nvidia announced a $2 billion investment in Lumentum, and another $2 billion in Coherent for OCS.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">OCS, meanwhile, provides a way to make optical more efficient for long flows between two destinations, and gives data centers a new way to configure optical interconnect. “When you&#8217;re trying to do all these memory-latency-sensitive things, you want to reduce the number of hops, and being purely in the optical domain does help,” Aguilar noted.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">Additionally, new alliances are forming. For instance, Lightmatter recently joined Nvidia’s NVLink ecosystem. But work remains. </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><span data-contrast="none">“Many companies are currently evaluating this option, and from a technology point of view, it makes a lot of sense,” said Ewald Liess, senior vice president of sales and business development at </span><a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/signatureip/">SignatureIP</a><span data-contrast="none">. “But with production costs and reliability, there are plenty of challenges to be solved.”</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>

		<title>DDR5 9600 RDIMMs: Raising The Performance Benchmark For Server Memory</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/ddr5-9600-rdimms-raising-the-performance-benchmark-for-server-memory/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/ddr5-9600-rdimms-raising-the-performance-benchmark-for-server-memory/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Zaman Mollah]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 13 Aug 2026 07:08:19 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[A Bit About Memory]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Blogs - LPHP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[agentic AI]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>The ability to move and manage data efficiently is a defining challenge for data center architects.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/ddr5-9600-rdimms-raising-the-performance-benchmark-for-server-memory/">DDR5 9600 RDIMMs: Raising The Performance Benchmark For Server Memory</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The rapid evolution of AI, high-performance computing (HPC) and cloud infrastructure is forcing every component of the server architecture to scale. While much attention has focused on processors and accelerators, memory is one of the most critical determinants of overall system performance. As CPU core counts continue to climb and AI workloads become increasingly memory intensive, the ability to move and manage data efficiently is a defining challenge for data center architects. This reality is helping drive the next step in server memory evolution: DDR5 RDIMMs operating at 9600 MT/s.</p>
<p>For years, system designers have depended on advances in memory bandwidth to keep pace with growing computational demands. Each generation of server processors has introduced additional cores, larger caches and more sophisticated processing capabilities. Yet without corresponding improvements in memory performance, these processors risk spending more time waiting for data than executing workloads.</p>
<p>The emergence of agentic AI as a mainstream data center workload has amplified this challenge. Unlike traditional enterprise applications, agentic AI services operate continuously, processing large datasets and managing complex decision-making workflows in real time. These workloads generate sustained pressure on memory subsystems, requiring higher bandwidth, larger memory pools and efficient power delivery to maintain system throughput.</p>
<p>Higher-speed DDR5 RDIMMs allow processors to access data more rapidly, reducing bottlenecks and improving utilization of expensive compute resources. This is particularly important in environments where large numbers of processor cores must simultaneously access memory. As servers scale upward, maintaining balanced performance across compute, memory and I/O subsystems becomes essential.</p>
<p>The move to DDR5 9600 provides a substantial increase in available memory bandwidth, enabling systems to sustain higher levels of workload concurrency and improve performance across data-intensive applications. But pushing memory speeds to 9600 MT/s is not simply a matter of increasing frequency. Each successive step in DDR5 performance introduces new challenges related to signal integrity, timing accuracy, power delivery and thermal management.</p>
<p>As data rates rise, electrical margins shrink. Small variations in clock timing, signal quality or voltage stability that were manageable at lower speeds can become significant barriers to reliable operation. Maintaining clean timing relationships between the processor, buffer devices and DRAM components requires increasingly sophisticated memory subsystem design.</p>
<p>This challenge has elevated the importance of supporting memory interface components that operate alongside the DRAM devices themselves. Functions such as clock distribution, power regulation, configuration management and telemetry become increasingly critical to achieving reliable operation at advanced data rates.</p>
<p>DDR5 RDIMMs incorporate extensive monitoring and management capabilities that allow systems to maintain optimal operating conditions and identify issues before they become failures. Temperature monitoring, power management and module telemetry provide valuable visibility into memory subsystem health while helping maintain consistent operation across large server fleets.</p>
<p>These capabilities become increasingly important as memory bandwidth, capacity and power density continue to rise. Advanced server platforms must deliver maximum performance without compromising reliability, making intelligent monitoring and control mechanisms essential components of the memory architecture.</p>
<p>As a result, memory design is becoming a multidisciplinary exercise that combines high-speed signaling, power engineering, thermal management and systems-level optimization. For system architects, the objective is clear: deliver more bandwidth, greater capacity and improved efficiency while maintaining the reliability required by enterprise and hyperscale deployments. The transition to DDR5 9600 represents a continuation of this ongoing trend.</p>
<p>Rambus supports this transition with a complete DDR5 9600 Server Memory Chipset that combines the 6<sup>th</sup>-generation DDR5 Registering Clock Driver, Power Management IC (PMIC 5030), SPD Hub and Temperature Sensor ICs in a comprehensive solution. By providing coordinated clocking, power management, configuration and telemetry functions, the chipset helps simplify module design, accelerate validation and maintain robust signal and power integrity at advanced DDR5 speeds. As server memory continues to scale, an integrated chipset approach can help module manufacturers, OEMs and hyperscalers bring next-generation platforms to market more efficiently while delivering the bandwidth, reliability and manageability demanded by AI and data-intensive workloads.</p>
<h3>Additional link</h3>

</ul>

		<item>
		<title>What Self-Verifying Means In Agentic EDA Workflows And Why It Matters</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/what-self-verifying-means-in-agentic-eda-workflows-and-why-it-matters/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/what-self-verifying-means-in-agentic-eda-workflows-and-why-it-matters/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Emma-Jane Crozier]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 13 Aug 2026 07:07:35 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Best Of Both: LP & HP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Blogs - LPHP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[agentic AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI in EDA]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[domain grounding]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[EDA]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[library characterization]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Siemens]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24280055</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Grounding agent decisions in their output is what transforms orchestration into something engineers can build on with confidence.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/what-self-verifying-means-in-agentic-eda-workflows-and-why-it-matters/">What Self-Verifying Means In Agentic EDA Workflows And Why It Matters</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Last month, we covered the architectural decisions behind a <a href="https://semiengineering.com/the-architecture-decisions-behind-a-production-ready-eda-ai-agent/">production-ready EDA AI agent</a>: domain grounding, scalable orchestration across a fragmented tool ecosystem, native interpretation of EDA data formats, and security at the execution layer. These are the foundations upon which successful agentic workflows for EDA are built, but the next layer is something that all engineers will ask about: trust. When an agent is executing a long-running EDA workflow autonomously, making countless interdependent decisions across multiple tools without interruption, how do you know the results can be trusted?</p>
<h2>Why deterministic physics-based EDA engines matter</h2>
<p>The answer is physics-based EDA engine verification. Physics-based, deterministic EDA engines deliver trusted, signoff-quality results and define the ground truth against which every EDA AI agent decision is validated. Every decision the agent makes is checked against the physics of the design before the next step begins, not at the end of the workflow or after an entire run completes, but continuously, at every step, against the same engines engineers have trusted for decades. Grounding agent decisions in their output is what transforms orchestration into something engineers can build on with confidence.</p>
<p>Why does this matter in EDA? In semiconductor and PCB design, there is no room for error and no tolerance for delay. Every RTL block, every SPICE simulation, every Liberty file matters. Tapeout dates are fixed, respins are expensive, and missed market windows do not come back. For agents operating autonomously across these workflows, there is zero margin for unverified decisions.</p>
<h2>How EDA engines and agents work together</h2>
<p>The interface between an agent and an EDA engine is fundamentally different from the interface a human designer uses, and building that interface required adding additional capabilities at the orchestration level specifically to interact with agents.</p>
<p>When a human designer is interacting with an EDA tool, they do not need to know all the internals of the engine and what the results are at that level of granularity. An agent, on the other hand, can take advantage of all of that information to reason, act, check with the tool, get feedback, and converge on the correct result. That is what makes continuous physics-based verification possible: the agent is in a continuous cycle with the tools themselves, generating data, verifying it, and if it is going off track, correcting before moving forward.</p>
<p>Agent Skills encode domain knowledge as executable playbooks, giving the agent not just the steps to follow but the context to execute them correctly, with validation built into every step. A scalable MCP architecture enables dynamic tool discovery and orchestration across Siemens&#8217; full EDA portfolio, from high-level synthesis with Catapult, verification with Questa One and Veloce, and custom IC design and verification with Solido, through to physical implementation with Aprisa, signoff verification with Calibre and design-for-test with Tessent, as well as 3D IC integration with Innovator3D IC and PCB design with Xpedition, mitigating context saturation as workflows expand.</p>
<p>The engineer remains in the process throughout. They can see what the agent is doing and the steps it is taking, and where the agent has done something incorrectly, they can augment it, storing that correction as new institutional knowledge in Agent Skills files that then go on to improve every subsequent agentic run. Agent Skills can also be configured to request human-in-the-loop approval before executing consequential steps, for example, checking with the engineer before launching a 5000-core SPICE job or a full DRC run.</p>
<h2>What an autonomous, self-verifying workflow looks like in practice</h2>
<p><a href="https://news.siemens.com/en-us/siemens-nvidia-dac-2026/">At DAC 2026, Siemens announced self-verifying, long-running EDA AI agents for semiconductor and PCB design, combining Siemens EDA expertise and software with NVIDIA AI infrastructure</a>. Library characterization with Solido Characterization Suite was one of the workflows demonstrated.</p>
<p>Library characterization has historically been one of the most labor-intensive steps in advanced node design and an extremely important one to later stage design phases. Generating and verifying Liberty files across process corners for standard cell and custom IP libraries typically demands multiple full-time engineers, weeks of runtime, and constant manual intervention.</p>
<p>In the demo shown at DAC, the agent receives a single instruction: “Characterize my libraries across all PVTs. Verify, debug, and fix any problems. I am going to bed and will not be available to answer any questions. Resolve any issues on your own.” Then it runs. When it encounters a problem, skill files guide the automated debug sequence. The agent identifies the issue, resolves it independently, and continues without escalation or handoff. Config setup that once consumed hours now takes minutes, pipecleaning that stretched across days wraps up in hours, and the full flow, previously a weeks-long effort, completes in days. Token costs are reduced by approximately 5X to 10X through NeMo Switchyard and Nemotron models, with an additional 25% reduction from NeMo Gym-based optimization of Agent Skills and MCP tools, delivering an overall 10 times faster autonomous characterization workflow, with every decision continuously validated against physics-based EDA engines at every step.</p>
<h2>From autonomous tasks to trusted engineering outcomes</h2>
<p>Over the past twelve months, each step in Siemens’ agentic EDA journey was a prerequisite for the next: domain grounding, scalable orchestration, and continuous physics-based validation. Physics-based EDA engine verification is the layer that completes the architecture, because it is what allows engineering organizations to move from autonomous task orchestration toward continuously validated engineering outcomes. The result is self-verifying, long-running EDA AI agents that engineers can trust with their most demanding workflows.</p>
<p><strong>To find out more:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a0UtM7bPKts&amp;t=91s">Watch the library characterization demo to see the autonomous EDA workflow in action</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G8181WBDp0Q">Hear the DAC conversation with Tiff in Tech: how Siemens EDA and NVIDIA are building the AI-native electronic design flow</a></li>

</ul>

		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Sharad Chole]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 13 Aug 2026 07:06:43 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - LPHP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Inside Edge AI Processing]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[VLM]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24280045</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Vision-only edge processors are giving way to systems where LLMs, VLMs, and generative features sit alongside traditional perception networks. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/packet-based-npus-in-the-llm-era-from-compute-bound-cnns-to-memory-bound-edge-and-automotive-workloads/">Packet-Based NPUs In The LLM Era: From Compute-Bound CNNs To Memory-Bound Edge And Automotive Workloads</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Many Semiconductor Engineering readers know the basic story behind Expedera’s Origin NPU IP architecture: packets instead of layers, higher MAC utilization, and less gratuitous movement of activations to external memory. What’s changing now is the workload mix. Vision-only edge processors are giving way to systems where LLMs, VLMs and generative features sit alongside traditional perception networks in smartphones, vehicles and embedded gateways.</p>
<p>In terms of NPU design, what are the implications when the dominant edge workloads stop being purely compute-bound CNNs and start looking like memory-bound transformers with large KV caches—especially in safety-critical automotive contexts?</p>
<h2>Workload inversion: CNNs vs LLMs/VLMs</h2>
<p>The first lens shift is recognizing the inversion in bottlenecks.</p>
<p>For CNN-based vision workloads (YOLO-class detectors, MobileNet-style classifiers, segmentation networks), the dominant constraint has historically been compute. Weights are reused, the execution is largely stateless at inference time, and accelerators were designed around maximizing MAC throughput within a given area and power envelope. Expedera’s packet-based scheduling improved MAC utilization and reduced DDR traffic by distributing work across packets rather than monolithic layers.</p>
<p>LLMs and VLMs change the story. As Expedera and others have been highlighting, prefill can still be heavy on arithmetic, but decode quickly becomes dominated by KV cache access and enlarged parameter sets with low effective reuse. The result is a workload that is increasingly memory-bound, not compute-bound, particularly when models are running in resource-constrained edge and in-vehicle environments.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24280046" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Expedera_Packet-Based-NPUs-LLM-Era-fig1.jpg?resize=619%2C128&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="619" height="128" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Expedera_Packet-Based-NPUs-LLM-Era-fig1.jpg?w=619&amp;ssl=1 619w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Expedera_Packet-Based-NPUs-LLM-Era-fig1.jpg?resize=300%2C62&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Expedera_Packet-Based-NPUs-LLM-Era-fig1.jpg?resize=600%2C124&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 619px) 100vw, 619px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Increased runtime inference complexity with LLMs.</strong></p>
<p>Moreover, CNN-centric NPUs were built for stateless, parallel, compute-bound inference, while VLM transformer decodes are now limited by memory behavior—KV cache size, access patterns, and bandwidth—not by the nominal TOPS rating on the datasheet.</p>
<h2>Packets in a memory-bound world</h2>
<p>Given this workload inversion, we looked at whether the packet abstraction that worked well for CNNs could be extended across transformer blocks and KV cache access, and co-designed hardware and software around LLM/VLM behavior rather than treating them as “just another model.”</p>
<p>At a high level, the engine:</p>
<ul>
<li>Scales to <strong>128 TFLOPS in a single core</strong>, and to <strong>PetaFLOPS</strong> with multi-core configurations, but does so in a way that keeps memory behavior central rather than incidental.</li>
<li>Uses <strong>discrete processing blocks</strong> for feed-forward, attention and vector operations, with packets routed across these blocks according to the network’s structure and the current phase (prefill vs decode).</li>
<li>Maintains the original promise: models run “as trained,” with <strong>no retraining and no accuracy reduction</strong>, while packetization and scheduling are managed within the hardware/software stack.</li>
</ul>
<p>The critical data point for LLMs is memory movement. We found that, compared to alternative approaches, packet-based processing can reduce external memory moves by more than 75% for Llama 3.2 1B and Qwen2 1.5B—networks that are representative of real embedded LLM deployments rather than toy examples.</p>
<p>Even in highly memory-bound scenarios, we’ve seen the architecture can deliver “thousands of effective TFLOPS” and “dozens of tokens per second per mm² of silicon,” pointing to a practical balance between compute and memory rather than an extreme in either direction.</p>
<h2>Edge and automotive implications: Latency, privacy, and power</h2>
<p>For edge and automotive systems, the packet story in LLM/VLM workloads translates directly into system-level constraints.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Latency and privacy.</strong> Running LLM inference locally reduces end-to-end latency and keeps in-cabin or on-device data out of the cloud, which is increasingly a requirement for both user experience and regulatory reasons.</li>
<li><strong>Memory and power budgets.</strong> In vehicles, edge nodes and mobile devices, memory is heavily constrained. Streaming KV cache to DDR or HBM on every decode step quickly becomes a power and cost problem. Packet-based scheduling that reduces external memory moves and increases local reuse translates into more tokens per second within a given power budget.</li>
<li><strong>Heterogeneous workload coexistence.</strong> Automotive SoCs need to run perception, driver monitoring, infotainment, and now generative features together. An NPU family that treats CNNs and LLMs as first-class citizens—rather than bolting LLM support onto a CNN-optimized core—simplifies platform design and reduces the need for separate accelerators.</li>
</ul>
<p>The recent “Best Edge AI Processor IP” award for Origin Evolution in the 2026 Edge AI and Vision Product of the Year Awards highlights the importance of a systems approach to solving the memory and power bottlenecks that prevent real-world deployment of GenAI at the edge, rather than just higher peak compute metrics.</p>
<h2>EDA and architecture: Modeling prefill and decode separately</h2>
<p>For EDA teams, the interesting part is less about packets as a concept and more about how to model and optimize prefill and decode phases explicitly.</p>
<p>Origin Evolution treats prefill and decode differently:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Prefill</strong> still wants high arithmetic throughput—matrix-multiply-heavy, closer to classic CNN behavior but with larger models.</li>
<li><strong>Decode</strong> is dominated by KV cache reads, memory streaming, and smaller per-step compute, potentially distributed across packets in a way that reduces external memory pressure and spreads work across attention and vector blocks.</li>
</ul>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24280047" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Expedera_Packet-Based-NPUs-LLM-Era-fig2.jpg?resize=780%2C294&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="780" height="294" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Expedera_Packet-Based-NPUs-LLM-Era-fig2.jpg?w=780&amp;ssl=1 780w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Expedera_Packet-Based-NPUs-LLM-Era-fig2.jpg?resize=300%2C113&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Expedera_Packet-Based-NPUs-LLM-Era-fig2.jpg?resize=768%2C289&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Expedera_Packet-Based-NPUs-LLM-Era-fig2.jpg?resize=600%2C226&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 780px) 100vw, 780px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 2: Inference event timeline comparison.</strong></p>
<p>Packet streams and discrete blocks make it possible to:</p>
<ul>
<li>Build performance and bandwidth models that differentiate between prefill and decode, rather than lumping transformer inference into a single average profile.</li>
<li>Explore cache hierarchy and streaming interface parameters (DRAM/HBM width, SRAM size, partitioning) against real KV cache access patterns, tuned per phase.</li>
<li>Analyze worst-case latency and bandwidth impact in safety-critical automotive workloads where LLM or VLM features are part of the human-machine interface or driver monitoring stack.</li>
</ul>
<p>The packet abstraction remains the foundation, but system designers can think of packets as <strong>units of LLM/VLM behavior</strong>—scheduled across phase-specific blocks and cache hierarchies—rather than only as CNN layer fragments.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24280048" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Expedera_Packet-Based-NPUs-LLM-Era-fig3.jpg?resize=431%2C450&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="431" height="450" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Expedera_Packet-Based-NPUs-LLM-Era-fig3.jpg?w=431&amp;ssl=1 431w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Expedera_Packet-Based-NPUs-LLM-Era-fig3.jpg?resize=287%2C300&amp;ssl=1 287w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Expedera_Packet-Based-NPUs-LLM-Era-fig3.jpg?resize=24%2C24&amp;ssl=1 24w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 431px) 100vw, 431px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 3: Packets – a unique approach to AI optimization.</strong></p>
<h2>Out-of-the-box compatibility and software-first flows</h2>
<p>From a software and EDA tooling perspective, another lens is compatibility.</p>
<p>Origin Evolution’s stack is built to ingest networks from HuggingFace, Llama.cpp, TVM and others, while supporting full integer and floating-point precisions, mixed modes, layer fusion/fission, and centralized control of multiple cores at the chip or chiplet level.</p>
<p>The practical point is that packetization is not a new programming model for users. In practice, existing trained models can be dropped onto the hardware with no reduction in accuracy and no retraining requirements, and that packetization happens in the compiler/runtime path.</p>
<p>For EDA and verification teams working in increasingly software-first procurement environments, this matters:</p>
<ul>
<li>It reduces the need for bespoke hardware-specific rewrites in the ML stack.</li>
<li>It allows performance modeling and regression testing against reference implementations (e.g., Llama 3, Qwen 2) without rebuilding networks for each architecture.</li>
<li>It aligns with the trend in automotive and mobile platforms where NPU IP is evaluated not just on microarchitecture, but on how fast and safely it can run real open-source models.</li>
</ul>
<h2>Looking ahead</h2>
<p>For edge AI designs, the open questions are less about whether packets work—they clearly do for CNNs—and more about how the architecture eases the complexity of modeling, scheduling, and verification across heterogeneous AI workloads. As GenAI features move into cars and edge devices at scale, those questions will likely determine which accelerator architectures actually make it into production and which remain confined to benchmark slides.</p>

		<title>Is Pergrammable A Word?</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/is-pergrammable-a-word/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/is-pergrammable-a-word/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Steve Roddy]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 13 Aug 2026 07:05:36 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - LPHP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Embedded ML Design]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[GPNPU]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[NPU]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[PPA]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[programmability]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Quadric]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24280081</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>SoC architects need AI silicon that is both highly efficient and fully programmable.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/is-pergrammable-a-word/">Is Pergrammable A Word?</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The price tag to invest in bespoke silicon for devices such as mobile phones, automobiles, laptops, or edge agentic token servers is enormous. Leading-edge SoCs can cost more than $200M to design, verify, and validate over a two-to-three-year development period. Semiconductor and systems companies making that level of investment want those new chips to have long production lifespans to deliver a solid return on investment (ROI).</p>
<p>But ensuring a solid ROI requires the design team to not only build competitive silicon for today&#8217;s known requirements, but also anticipate future needs as markets shift. That anticipation problem was always hard; in the age of AI, it has become nearly impossible.</p>
<p>In virtually all of the end markets that drive high-volume SoC design — automotive, mobile, PC, industrial, robotics, networking — running AI models on device is increasingly mandatory. Yet predicting which AI models will be the hot flavor of the month when the new silicon is finally ready to ship is an impossible task. The state of the art in AI changes monthly, sometimes weekly. A two-year silicon design cycle might see the state of the art in the target market segment change five, ten, or more times before the chip ever reaches a customer&#8217;s board.</p>
<h2>What the architect is actually asking for</h2>
<p>The SoC architect laying out requirements for a new chip&#8217;s AI subsystem has, by necessity, learned to demand two things simultaneously: performance and programmability.</p>
<p>Performance — or, in the vernacular of the semiconductor world, being performant — means the AI subsystem can crunch through inference workloads efficiently: high throughput, low power, low latency. For a fixed bill of materials and power budget, efficiency is everything.</p>
<p>Programmability means the chip can be updated in the field to run AI models that haven&#8217;t been invented yet, models trained on architectures and operators that didn&#8217;t exist when the SoC was taped out. Models that will only emerge years from now, on some future Tuesday when a research team publishes something that immediately rewrites the rules.</p>
<p>Both of these requirements are real and both are non-negotiable, and yet the universe of AI processor licensors has, for the past several years, never offered a solution that didn’t compromise one or the other.</p>
<h2>The standard NPU architecture and its fatal flaw</h2>
<p>Walk the floor of any semiconductor IP trade show and you will hear the same pitch, repeated by a dozen different exhibitors with a dozen different logos: &#8220;Our solution pairs a high-performance matrix accelerator with a programmable core, giving your SoC both efficiency and flexibility.&#8221;</p>
<p>The accelerator handles the heavy lifting, the big, regular matrix operations that dominate the popular benchmark models. The programmable core (a CPU, DSP, or GPU, depending on the vendor&#8217;s legacy product line) handles everything else.</p>
<p>It sounds reasonable. And for a brief window in time — roughly 2019 to 2022, when the dominant inference benchmarks were ResNet variants and MobileNet derivatives — it worked well enough. The accelerator handled 90-plus percent of the compute, and the programmable core handled the thin tail of operators the accelerator couldn&#8217;t touch. It was a manageable partitioning problem.</p>
<p>Then came transformers, then large language models and their edge-targeted descendants, then vision-language-action models. Each wave brought new operator types, new graph topologies, new memory access patterns, many of which the fixed-function accelerator was never designed to handle. Suddenly the &#8220;manageable partitioning problem&#8221; became a performance cliff. Workloads that should have run on the accelerator landed instead on the programmable core, which promptly ran them at a fraction of the speed. Running them was academic; technically they ran, but so slowly as to be functionally useless.</p>
<p>That is the fatal flaw baked into every paired architecture: the algorithm runs on either the performant engine or the programmable engine — never both, and never simultaneously. You get one or the other. The more of the workload you push to the accelerator, the less flexible your silicon becomes. But the more you rely on the programmable core to handle new operators, the more performance you sacrifice.</p>
<h2>A tell the industry has been ignoring</h2>
<p>There is an obvious question that nobody in the industry has asked loudly enough:</p>
<p><i>If the programmable cores that these vendors pair with their accelerators were truly useful for running AI workloads, why would they pair them with accelerators at all? Why not simply sell the programmable core alone and let designers use it to run their AI models directly?</i></p>
<p>The answer, of course, is that no vendor makes that pitch because it would immediately reveal the performance gap. The programmable cores they bundle into their &#8220;hybrid&#8221; solutions are legacy architectures built for signal processing, control code, or general-purpose computation. They’re not designed for matrix-heavy AI inference and they never were. The accelerator is not a complement to the programmable core, it’s a confession that the programmable core cannot do the job.</p>
<p>What this market is selling as a unified solution is actually two products duct-taped together, each compensating for the other&#8217;s weakness, and neither doing the job the SoC architect actually needs done.</p>
<h2>Introducing a word that should exist</h2>
<p>The English language has a long tradition of coining new words when existing vocabulary fails to describe something real. We borrow, blend, compress, and invent. And so, with apologies to Merriam-Webster:</p>
<blockquote><p><strong>pergrammable</strong></p>
<p><i>/ pər-ˈgra-mə-bəl /   adj.</i></p>
<p><i>Of a processor architecture: simultaneously and inseparably exhibiting both high computational efficiency and full software programmability, such that neither quality is sacrificed for the other.</i></p></blockquote>
<p>Pergrammable is not performant OR programmable. It’s not an accelerator bolted to a legacy core. It’s a single processing architecture that delivers both properties simultaneously, from the same silicon, executing the same instruction stream.</p>
<p>That’s the thing the SoC architect has been asking for, it just didn&#8217;t have a name.</p>
<h2>The only pergrammable NPU on the market</h2>
<p>Quadric&#8217;s Chimera GPNPU is pergrammable. It’s not a marketing claim layered on top of a conventional paired architecture. The pergrammability of Chimera is a direct consequence of how the processor was designed from the first principles up.</p>
<p>Chimera&#8217;s instruction set architecture is purpose-built and matrix-native, conceived from day one to execute AI inference workloads at high efficiency while remaining fully programmable by software developers writing in C++ or Python. The matrix compute and the programmable control aren’t separate engines connected by a bus and coordinated by a partitioning compiler; they’re unified into a single execution pipeline, running a single instruction stream.</p>
<p>The practical consequences of this are significant:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Any model runs. </strong>A new AI model — including operators that didn&#8217;t exist at tape-out — can be ported to Chimera as a software update. No hardware revision, no NRE, no silicon respin.</li>
<li><strong>No performance cliff. </strong>Because there is no partition between a performant engine and a programmable engine, operators run at full matrix throughput regardless of their novelty. The performance doesn’t degrade for new workloads.</li>
<li><strong>Silicon that compounds. </strong>The chip designed today does not depreciate as AI models evolve, it compounds. The same silicon can run models published years after tape-out at performance levels that match or exceed what a fixed-function accelerator achieves today.</li>
</ul>
<p>This is why Quadric describes Chimera as a living platform. The stack is software. New AI capabilities ship as software updates to existing silicon and the chip doesn&#8217;t age the way a fixed-function accelerator ages.</p>
<p>Chimera scales from 1 TOPS to more than 6,400 TOPS in multi-chiplet configurations. It supports convolutional networks, transformers, state-space models, VLA world models, and whatever architecture the AI research community invents next year. All on the same silicon, using the same toolchain, and programmable by the SoC customer&#8217;s own software team without requiring Quadric&#8217;s involvement or a new licensing arrangement.</p>
<p>The competing solutions in this market will continue to iterate their accelerators, releasing second-generation and third-generation hardwired engines that are each optimized for the models that were popular at the time the accelerator was designed. Each iteration will be a short-term fix for a structural problem that cannot be solved by adding another layer of fixed function to an architecture built on the wrong foundation.</p>
<p>The SoC architect doesn&#8217;t have to wait for those vendors to find a better answer. A pergrammable solution already exists. It&#8217;s called Chimera.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/is-pergrammable-a-word/">Is Pergrammable A Word?</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<title>What Will It Take To Deploy CPO At Scale?</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/what-will-it-take-to-deploy-cpo-at-scale/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/what-will-it-take-to-deploy-cpo-at-scale/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[James Nguyen]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 13 Aug 2026 07:04:42 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - LPHP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Co-Packaged Optics Insights]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Ayar Labs]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[co-packaged optics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[CPO]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[data centers]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[networking]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[scale-out]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Scale-Up]]></category>
